title: From Cave Wall to Picture Book
question: Daddy, who drew us?
placard: My son had learned to read, and to talk in full sentences, by the time he was two. One morning, having just read The Arabian Nights, he looked up and asked me this. It is a bigger question than it sounds. Somebody drew Hairy Maclary, and somebody, a very long time ago, drew the first picture of all. This room walks from the oldest hands on a cave wall to the picture books on his shelf.
summary: How people have drawn and painted, from hand stencils and the Lascaux caves to the pencil, the rubber, Peter Rabbit, Crayola and ink made from oak galls.

title: Chapter One
question: What is the oldest book in the world?
placard: Books are the gateway to almost everything. Through them we learn about other cultures, far-off places, history, politics, nature and science, and we hear the tales people have carried for centuries. This chapter begins with the oldest dated printed book, then asks some bigger questions: which is the longest, which sells the most, how books are made, and how many there are.
summary: Books are the gateway to learning and stories. This chapter begins with the oldest dated printed book and covers the hornbook, how books are made, the longest and best-selling books, and how many there are.

title: From Quill to Keyboard
question: Did you use to write on a typewriter, Dad?
placard: Yes, I did — and correction fluid too, the cheaper kind. To my son, the past is one flat place where I might as well have been chiselling stone tablets. This gallery gives it some depth: how we got from reeds and feathers to the keys under your fingers.
summary: How writing and printing evolved, from papyrus and goose quills to movable type, the typewriter and correction fluid.

title: Folk Tales
question: Why did Hansel leave a trail?
placard: Long before these stories were printed, they were told aloud, in kitchens and by fires, and they changed a little with every telling. This room follows some of the trails they leave behind: crumbs, a red hood and a ball of thread.
summary: Hansel and Gretel, Little Red Riding Hood and Theseus in the Labyrinth: old stories that were told aloud long before they were printed, and the trails they leave behind.

title: Names That Nearly Were
question: Was Xbox always called Xbox?
placard: My son and I were watching a documentary about the Xbox when we learned the name was only ever meant to be temporary. It turns out a lot of famous names were nearly something else entirely — some ridiculous, some forgotten, some saved by a misheard word or a trademark search that ran out of time.
summary: Famous names that began as placeholders, near-misses and happy accidents: Xbox, Bluetooth, Sherlock Holmes, James Bond, Amazon and more.

title: Back from the Brink
question: Can an animal come back once it's nearly gone?
placard: Sometimes the answer is yes. Each animal in this room fell to a handful: four kestrels, five robins, a few dozen condors. Then someone decided not to give up. These are true stories of stubborn people, lucky breaks and second chances, and of how close some of them came to ending the other way.
summary: Animals, and one river, brought back from the edge of extinction: the Mauritius kestrel, Old Blue the robin, the California condor, the Arabian oryx and more.

title: Wheels and Wings
question: When was the bicycle invented?
placard: My son asked me this one. The answer is 1817, and the first bicycle had no pedals. From there the trail runs on wheels of every kind, along the first railway, and then, thanks to two brothers who mended bicycles, up into the air.
summary: How we learned to get about: the first bicycle, the penny-farthing, roller skates, skateboards, the Rocket, the first car journey, the hot air balloon, the Wright brothers and the helicopter.

title: What Things Are Made Of
question: Why is glass see-through if it's made from sand?
placard: Sand is gritty and you can't see through a bucketful of it, so how does it end up as a window? It is a simple question with a surprising answer. From there this room looks at the stuff our everyday things are made of, and at the accidents, stubborn experiments and walks with the dog that gave us them.
summary: The surprising stories behind everyday materials: why glass is clear, lightning glass, safety glass, Pyrex, Gorilla Glass, stainless steel and Velcro.

title: Where Words Come From
question: Why do we say it's raining cats and dogs?
placard: My son asked me this one, and I had to admit I didn't know. It turns out nobody does, not for certain, and that is half the fun. Every word we use has a story behind it: some we know, some we can only guess at, and some that people tell even though they aren't true. This room collects a few of the best.
summary: The stories behind everyday words and sayings: raining cats and dogs, clue, daisy, muscle, nice, goodbye, hello and the computer bug.

title: Weird Biology
question: Why does the hair on our arms and legs stop growing, but not the hair on our head?
placard: Bodies are strange. They grow hair that knows when to stop, make goosebumps for fur we no longer have, and shrink a little every day. This room starts with one of the best body questions I have been asked, and goes on to some of the oddest things your own body does without asking you first.
summary: The odd things bodies do: hair that stops growing, goosebumps, wrinkly bath fingers, record-breaking hiccups, sun sneezes, brain freeze, being taller in the morning and babies' extra bones.

title: From Steam Wagon to Supercar
question: When was the first car made?
placard: This one wasn't a question. My son told me when the first car was made. But, as with most firsts, the more you look, the more there is to find: a steam wagon that may have knocked down a wall, a man walking in front with a red flag, a car named after a little girl, and a tractor maker who was told to stick to tractors.
summary: The story of cars, from Cugnot's steam wagon and the Red Flag Act to Benz's 1886 patent, the electric record-breaker, Mercedes, the windscreen wiper, the Model T, the seat belt and Lamborghini.

title: How Do We Know?
question: If you've always called a traffic light red, how would you know you see it differently?
placard: It's a brilliant question, because the honest answer is: you might not, unless you compare notes with someone else. That turns out to be how a lot of knowledge works. Nobody has walked round the Earth with a tape measure, dug to its middle, or flown to the Sun. So how do we know? This room is about the clever, patient and sometimes lucky ways people found out.
summary: How we found out what we can't see for ourselves: colour blindness, whether your red is my red, what dogs see, the size of the Earth, the speed of light, helium on the Sun, the Earth's inner core and the age of the Earth.

title: Finding the Way
question: How do salmon swim thousands of miles and find the stream where they hatched?
placard: A salmon has no map, no compass and no one to ask. Yet after years at sea it swims home to the very stream where it began. It turns out the natural world is full of navigators like this: turtles, terns, butterflies, beetles and pigeons, and some remarkable people too. This room is about how they find their way.
summary: Amazing navigators: salmon and sea turtles that remember a magnetic address, the Arctic tern, a godwit's 11-day flight, monarch butterflies, dung beetles steering by the Milky Way, homing pigeons and Pacific wayfinders.

title: From Tinfoil to Streaming
question: Daddy, I can hear everything.
placard: This one wasn't a question. My son said it in wonder, and it was true. He has always loved sound, in whatever form it comes: with perfect pitch, he could imitate anything from a pigeon to the Wii jingle to the engine of every supercar. So this room follows sound itself: how people first caught it, sent it through the air, pressed it into discs, wound it onto tape, and finally squeezed it into the phone in your pocket.
summary: How we caught and carried sound: Edison's tinfoil, flat records and vinyl LPs, the wireless, the cassette, the Walkman, the CD, the MP3 and streaming, plus the mystery of perfect pitch.

title: Restless Earth
question: Can the ground really move?
placard: I walked up Parícutin once, and it was not a gentle walk. I cut my leg on the lava. Then, after we had walked the rim, we slid back down the ash on our feet, which was the fastest way down and the most fun. The ground under us had been a cornfield not long before. This room is about land that moves: a volcano that was born in a field, an island that rose out of the sea, and rocks that sail across a dry lake bed.
summary: Ground that is born, rises and moves: a volcano that grew in a cornfield, an island that came up out of the sea, and rocks that sail across a desert lake bed.

title: Why Don't We Float Away?
question: Why are we attached to the ground? Why don't we float into the air?
placard: It is one of the first questions most of us ask about gravity, and the answers are stranger than they sound. Gravity pulls on everything, including you, the chair you are sitting on and the air above it. Why it pulls is not the whole story. How hard it pulls depends on where you are, and an astronaut who floats in orbit is still being pulled by Earth. This room follows the pull from an apple, to the Moon, to the space station.
summary: Why we stay on the ground: the pull of gravity, why you would weigh a sixth as much on the Moon, and why astronauts float even though gravity is still strong.

title: Are We Waterproof?
question: Daddy, are we waterproof?
placard: My son asked this one, and I didn't know the answer, so we went looking. It turns out that skin, feathers and leaves all have their own ways of dealing with water. Some keep it out, some let it through, and some let it roll off. This room starts with our own skin, and then looks at a duck and a leaf.
summary: Are we waterproof? Our skin soaks up a little water and swells, birds oil their feathers to shed it, and the lotus leaf sheds it completely.

title: Bigger and Smaller
question: Why does Africa look so small?
placard: My son noticed that the map makes Africa look small and America look big. He was right, and it isn't a silly mistake. This room looks at the map most of us grew up with, why it stretches the world the way it does, and what other maps do instead.
summary: The world map most of us grew up with was made in 1569 for sailors, and it makes countries near the poles look far bigger than they are. Other maps show the land differently, and each one is a choice.

title: Board Games
question: Who really invented Monopoly?
placard: Many of the board games on our shelves are older than we are, and some are far older. This room starts with the game credited to one man but first patented by a woman, then follows the crumbs to a wartime murder mystery, a word game, a race game from India and chess.
summary: Monopoly, Cluedo, Scrabble, Ludo and chess: where the best-known board games came from, and who first thought of them.

title: Games for Every Age
question: Which games does every generation still play?
placard: Some games are played at every age, from a child's first game of Snap to a grown-up's turn at charades. This room looks at four that have crossed the generations, and where each one began.
summary: Snap, charades, Jenga and Twister: games that have lasted for generations, and how each one began.

title: Modern Entertainment
question: How much time do we spend looking at screens?
placard: Screens have become part of nearly every day, for children and grown-ups alike. This room looks at the latest survey figures, the consoles people own, and two games from the 1970s and 1980s that are still played around the table.
summary: How much time children and adults spend online and watching television, how many consoles have been sold, and two games from the 1970s and 1980s.

title: The Movie Room
question: How did television go from black and white to streaming?
placard: We used to watch programmes when they were broadcast, and rent films on tape. This room follows the picture from the first public television, through the videotape and the disc, to the streaming service on the sofa.
summary: From the first public television at Alexandra Palace to videotapes, DVDs and streaming: how we have watched programmes and films at home.

title: Magic and Magicians
question: How is a lady sawn in half?
placard: Magic is about a moment of wonder. This room looks at the performers who made it famous, the tricks that became legends, and the history behind the stage. It tells the story of the illusion, and does not explain how it is done.
summary: The great magicians and the tricks that made them famous, from the sawing illusion to the escape artist Houdini.

title: Musicals
question: Where did the musical begin?
placard: Some stories are best told with a song. This room follows the musical from the first show whose story depended on its songs, to the longest-running show on Broadway.
summary: From Show Boat in 1927 to The Phantom of the Opera: the musical, and the shows that changed how stories are sung.

title: The Theatre
question: Where did Shakespeare's plays first go on?
placard: Long before the cinema, a play took place in a room full of people, with no second take. This room looks at the Globe, the theatre that Shakespeare's company built on the south bank of the Thames.
summary: The Globe Theatre, built in 1599 for Shakespeare's company, and the fire that destroyed it.

title: Solo Singers
question: Who has sold the most records as a solo artist?
placard: One voice, one name on the poster. This room looks at the solo singers who have sold the most records, and the figures that make them count.
summary: Elvis Presley, the best-selling solo artist in the United States, and how sales figures are counted.

title: Groups and Bands
question: How many records have the Beatles sold?
placard: Some of the biggest names in music were groups of people playing together. This room looks at the bands who have sold the most records, and why the numbers are hard to pin down.
summary: The Beatles and other bands: the best-selling groups, and why their sales figures are disputed.
